# Proverbs 29 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## v. 1: *“A man who remains stiff-necked after much reproof will suddenly be shattered beyond recovery.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The “stiff neck” is a metaphor drawn from oxen that refuse the yoke (Gill). It describes someone who, despite repeated correction from parents, ministers, the Holy Spirit, or providential chastisements, hardens himself and despises all counsel. The destruction is sudden—“shattered” like a potter’s vessel (Jeremiah 19:11)—and without remedy: there is no healing, no cure, no pardon for such obstinate rejection of God’s warnings (comp. Hebrews 6:4). God’s patience is long but not endless. (Enduring Word, Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

- **Reformed emphasis:** Ligonier notes that receiving reproof is painful, but Christians should be quick to receive it because nothing can separate us from God’s love in Christ (Rom. 8:1). The verse is cited alongside Proverbs 27:6 (“Faithful are the wounds of a friend”) to show correction as a gift. (Ligonier, *Faithful Wounds*)
  - https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithful-wounds

- **Pulpit Homiletics (W. Clarkson)** traces five stages to spiritual ruin: (1) human disloyalty, (2) God’s summons to return, (3) human recusancy (refusal/delay), (4) God’s patience through various means, and (5) sudden, irremediable ruin. He notes that the end often comes without expectation or preparation. (Pulpit Commentary)
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 2: *“When the righteous flourish, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The community or nation benefits when the righteous are in authority; the people rejoice because justice, peace, and godliness are promoted. When the wicked rule, all suffer—lawlessness increases, freedoms diminish, and the people groan “both for the oppressions and mischiefs which they feel, and for the dreadful judgments of God which they justly fear” (Poole, cited in Enduring Word). G. Campbell Morgan commented that “to observe long issues is to be convinced of the absolute accuracy of the sentiment.”
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html

- **Matthew Henry:** The people have cause to rejoice or mourn as their rulers are righteous or wicked. (Henry’s Concise)
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/proverbs-29.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Public happiness depends on individual conduct—specifically, the religious character of those who govern. Quotes Hooker’s *Ecclesiastical Polity*: “Religion, unfeignedly lived, perfecteth man’s abilities unto all kinds of virtuous services in the commonwealth.” (Pulpit Homiletics)
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 3: *“A man who loves wisdom brings joy to his father, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The one who loves wisdom (especially the fear of God and Christ, “the Wisdom of God”) gladdens his father both temporally (he does not waste his inheritance) and spiritually. The companion of prostitutes wastes his substance and damns his soul (Gill). Ellicott notes this verse is “illustrated by the parable of the prodigal son” (Luke 15). Enduring Word quotes Adam Clarke: “Has there ever been a single case to the contrary?”
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Wisdom and virtue are inseparable in conduct—the French word *sage* means both wise and chaste. Joy to parents and waste through vice are the two contrasting effects. (Pulpit Homiletics)
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 4: *“By justice a king brings stability to the land, but a man who exacts tribute demolishes it.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** Justice (upright decisions in court, fair administration) establishes the land. The opposite is “he who receives gifts”—bribes that pervert judgment and overthrow the foundations of fairness and equality before the law. Bridges: “The best laws are of little use when they are badly administered.” The Hebrew phrase “a man of oblations” can also mean “a man of exactions”—one who imposes heavy taxes or tributes, bringing the people to distress and the state to ruin (Gill). The Puritan John Trapp called this “one piece of Solomon’s politics” with more good advice than “all Lypsius’s Beehive, or Machiavel’s Spider web.”
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm

- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** “A just king or ruler establishes the country by the exercise of justice; but he who accepts bribes overthrows it.” (Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary)
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-29.html

- **Pulpit:** God’s throne is founded on justice (Psalm 89:14); this alone is the foundation of stable national polity. The corruption of Samuel’s sons overthrew the theocracy; David’s just administration “bore up the pillars” of the land; Jehoiakim’s greed shook the kingdom (Jeremiah 22:18-19). (Pulpit Homiletics)
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 5: *“A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The flatterer (“a smooth boots…a butter-spoken man,” Trapp) spreads a hidden net. His tongue is divided from his heart—he flatters not to please but to deceive and profit himself (Clarke). The result is a snare into which the flattered neighbor stumbles. Bridges: “Oh, it is a cruel thing to flatter. The soul is often more exhausted and injured by disentangling itself from these nets than by the hottest contest with principalities and powers.” (Enduring Word, Gill, Pulpit)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

- **Pulpit Homiletics:** The kiss of the flatterer is more deadly than the hate of a foe. “When we are most praised for our discernment, we are apt to act most foolishly; for praise tends to cloud the understanding and pervert the judgment.” (Pulpit)
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 6: *“An evil man is caught by his own sin, but a righteous one sings and rejoices.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The evil man is snared by his own transgression—he cannot escape God’s wrath through repentance because he does not repent (Ellicott). His “jollity is but the hypocrisy of mirth” (Trapp). The righteous, however, “doth sing and rejoice”—being assured of God’s mercy, having a clear conscience, and the “peace of God” (Philippians 4:7) keeping his heart. Gill adds that the righteous man rejoices in Christ’s righteousness, in pardon through His blood, in all His offices, and in hope of glory. (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html

---

## v. 7: *“The righteous consider the cause of the poor, but the wicked have no regard for such concerns.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The righteous man “knows the judgment of the poor”—he acquaints himself thoroughly with their case and seeks justice for them (Gill). This is thoughtful compassion in action (Enduring Word). The wicked “does not understand such knowledge”—his ignorance is not intellectual but a willful, evil perversion (Waltke, cited in Enduring Word). Ellicott compares the wicked man’s indifference to Dives ignoring Lazarus at his gate.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm

- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** “The righteous have compassion for and seek to insure justice for the poor… but the wicked see no profit in the poor and care not what happens to them.” (Garner-Howes)
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-29.html

---

## v. 8: *“Mockers inflame a city, but the wise turn away anger.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** “Scornful men” (mockers, scoffers) “set a city aflame”—they fan passions like a flame, raising tumults and seditions (Ellicott, Gill). “Mocking is catching, as the pestilence, and no less pernicious to the whole country” (Trapp). Wise men, by their gentle counsels, turn away wrath—both human anger and divine judgment. G. Campbell Morgan called this “a fine motto for engraving on the walls of the Foreign Office of any nation.” (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html

---

## v. 9: *“If a wise man goes to court with a fool, there will be raving and laughing with no resolution.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The setting is likely a court of law (Garrett, cited in Enduring Word). However the wise man handles the fool—whether with sternness or gentleness—the fool responds with either rage or mocking laughter; “there is no rest,” no peace, no resolution. The fool will not be satisfied or convinced (Poole). The proverb teaches the wise to be cautious about contending with fools: all labour to reclaim a fool is lost, whatever methods one uses (Gill, citing Proverbs 27:22). (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html

---

## v. 10: *“Men of bloodshed hate a blameless man, but the upright care for his life.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** “The bloodthirsty hate the upright” because the blameless man’s life is a continual reproach to them—what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness? (Ellicott, citing 2 Corinthians 6:14). The “just” or upright, by contrast, “seek his soul”—they care for and defend the life of the blameless person. Gill notes that just magistrates will seek out the bloodthirsty to punish them, or the upright will pray for the spiritual welfare even of their persecutors. (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html

---

## v. 11: *“A fool vents all his anger, but a wise man holds it back.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** Literally, “a fool brings out all his wrath/spirit” at once—he cannot restrain it (Gill, Ellicott). The wise man “keepeth it in till afterwards”—he holds back his anger until a proper time or stills it entirely. Kidner notes the verb (used in Psalm 89:9 of stilling a storm) “speaks of anger overcome, not merely checked.” Trapp says the wise man keeps it “in an inner room, in the bottom and bosom of his mind, till he see a fit season.” (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html

---

## v. 12: *“If a ruler listens to lies, all his officials will be wicked.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** When a ruler shows he likes flattery and falsehood rather than unpleasant truths, his attendants will provide what he wishes (Ellicott). “Courtiers adjust themselves to the prince—when they see that deception and court flattery win the day, they learn how the game is played” (Ross, cited in Enduring Word). Poole adds: partly because the ruler chooses only such men for his service, and partly because they are corrupted by his example. (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html

---

## v. 13: *“The poor man and the oppressor have this in common: The LORD gives light to the eyes of both.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** A variation of Proverbs 22:2. “The Lord lighteneth both their eyes”—He gives the light of life to both (Psalm 13:4). To each, the poor man and the oppressor, God gives life; therefore the poor may remember that life with its sorrows will end, and the oppressor that God will take stern vengeance for oppression (Ellicott). G. Campbell Morgan: “All intelligence is a divine gift, whether it be used in righteousness or in wickedness. Sin is always the prostitution of a God-given power to base purposes” (cited in Enduring Word). (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 14: *“A king who judges the poor with fairness—his throne will be established forever.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The king who faithfully administers justice to the poor—showing no partiality for or against them—will have his throne established. The poor are made in God’s image and have God as their avenger (Garrett, cited in Enduring Word). The promise echoes Jeremiah 22:3-4. Trapp saw this pointing ultimately to the throne of the Messiah, “professedly the poor man’s patron” (Psalm 9:18-19). (Enduring Word, Ellicott)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm

- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** This reaches ultimate fulfillment in the administration of the LORD, the Judge of all (Psalm 72:4; Isaiah 11:4; Acts 17:31). (Garner-Howes)
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/proverbs-29.html

---

## v. 15: *“A rod of correction imparts wisdom, but a child left to himself disgraces his mother.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The rod (physical discipline) and reproof (verbal correction) together give wisdom and drive out foolishness (Gill, citing Proverbs 22:15). “A child left to himself”—allowed to wander unchecked like the wild ass (Job 39:5)—brings shame to his mother. Poole notes the mother is specifically named because her indulgence often spoils the child, and children commonly stand in least awe of their mothers. Bridges: “Discipline is the order of God’s government. Parents are his dispensers of it to their children.” (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html

---

## v. 16: *“When the wicked thrive, rebellion increases; but the righteous will see their downfall.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** When the wicked are multiplied or come into authority, transgression increases among the people—both because wicked rulers encourage sin by example and because more wicked people commit more sins. But the righteous “shall see their fall” with joy (Psalm 54:7), having long expected it (Psalm 73:18). Bridges: “The faithful Christian minister, conscious of his inability to stem the ever-flowing torrent of iniquity, would sink in despair but for the assured confidence that he is on the conquering side.” (Enduring Word, Gill, Ellicott)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 17: *“Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your soul.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** Proper correction brings ease of mind, freedom from anxious cares, and ultimately delight—through the child’s obedience, prudent behaviour, diligence, and fear of God (Gill). Enduring Word notes that God appeals to parental self-interest: if you will not correct your son for his own sake, do it because it is good for you. (Enduring Word, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html

---

## v. 18: *“Where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint; but blessed is he who keeps the Law.”*

**This is the most heavily discussed verse in the chapter, and the one where traditions differ most sharply.**

- **Traditional Reading (Older commentaries):** “Vision” (Hebrew *chazon*) means prophetic revelation—God’s revealed word through His prophets. When such revelation is absent, the people “perish” (KJV) or “cast off restraint” (NKJV)—the Hebrew verb *para‘* means to let loose, run wild, become ungovernable. Gill makes it explicitly about the public preaching of the Word: “where there is no preaching, men perish in their sins.” Matthew Henry: “How bare does a place look without Bibles and ministers!” The second line confirms this: “blessed is he who keeps the law”—the written Word. The contrast is between lawless chaos without revelation and blessed obedience within it.
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-2918-commentary
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/David Guzik):** Affirms the traditional reading: *chazon* means God’s great revelation, not visionary leadership. “The revelation in mind here is not the spontaneous word from a purported prophet. It is God’s great revelation, His revealed word through the Hebrew prophets and later the apostles and prophets who gave us the New Testament.” Guzik explicitly rejects the popular “visionary leadership” application. (Enduring Word)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/

- **Modern Evangelical Misapplication (critiqued by Reformed/Baptist):** Many church leaders have used the KJV rendering “where there is no vision, the people perish” to spiritualize their own strategies—vision statements, mission statements, strategic plans. The Gospel Coalition (Reformed/evangelical) directly critiques this: “Proverbs 29:18 is not about your big ideas.” The vision is *prophetic* vision—what God has revealed through biblical spokesmen. The vision, ultimately, is Jesus (Colossians 1:26). (The Gospel Coalition)
  - https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/proverbs-2918-is-not-about-your-big-ideas/

- **Desiring God (John Piper, Baptist/Reformed):** Piper applies the verse more broadly to “godly dreaming”—letting God stretch the imagination—while acknowledging “vision” means “a kind of revelation, a vision from God.” He says, “Where there is no vision, this God-directed dreaming, the people cast off restraint… What we need today are great dreamers.” This is a somewhat broader application than the strictly exegetical one. (Desiring God)
  - https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-battle-for-your-mind

- **Precept Austin (detailed exegesis):** Provides comprehensive analysis showing that *chazon* refers to divine communication to prophets (as in 1 Samuel 3:1), not individual goals or plans. The KJV “perish” is misleading—*para‘* means “cast off restraint,” not eternal perdition. The NET notes: “Without them [prophetic calls] the downward rush to anarchy and destruction would have been faster.” The phrase “blessed is he who keeps the law” shows that “law” parallels “vision”—both refer to God’s revealed Word. (Precept Austin)
  - https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-2918-commentary

- **Barnes’ Notes:** The word “vision” is “commonly used of the revelation of God’s will made to prophets. Compare Isaiah 1:1; Nahum 1:1.” When there was “no open vision” (1 Samuel 3:1), the people “perish”—are let loose, left to run wild. (Barnes, via StudyLight)
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/proverbs-29.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** There must be commanding religious teaching. “The great prophets of Israel were the great instructors of the people.” The Christian preacher has succeeded to the office of the Jewish prophet. “Woe to the nation if the supply of preachers ceases!” (Pulpit Homiletics)
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 19: *“A servant cannot be corrected by words alone; though he understands, he will not respond.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The idea is of someone with a slave-like mentality—not an honorable servant-hearted person. Such a one must be governed by sterner means than mere words; it is only fear of punishment that moves him. “Though he understands, he will not answer”—will not reply to the call or render obedience (Ellicott). The willing obedience of a son and the grudging obedience of a slave are contrasted in Romans 8:15. (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 20: *“Do you see a man who speaks in haste? There is more hope for a fool than for him.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The man “hasty in his words” is a special kind of fool—a “super-fool.” The ordinary fool (*kesîl*) is a dull, self-satisfied person who may yet learn better; but the rash, impulsive speaker has a harder task in governing his tongue (Ellicott, citing James 3:2). His hasty words rush out before thought can intervene. (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 21: *“A servant pampered from his youth will bring grief in the end.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** Ellicott renders it: “He that delicately bringeth up his servant from a child shall have him become his son at the length”—that is, the pampered servant forgets his position and becomes presumptuous, even dictatorial. The warning is against spoiling a servant (or employee) by over-indulgence, which breeds ingratitude. The Pulpit Commentary calls this “want of due severity in discipline”—“men are stung by the ingratitude or contumacy of those whom they had weakly petted.” (Ellicott, Pulpit, Gill)
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 22: *“An angry man stirs up dissension, and a hot-tempered man abounds in transgression.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The angry man stirs up strife wherever he goes; wrath is the “very hot bed of transgression and every evil work” (Pulpit). Ellicott asks, “For what will he not say and do when overcome by anger?” (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill, Pulpit)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 23: *“A man’s pride will bring him low, but a humble spirit will obtain honor.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** Pride brings a person low by God’s design—God resists the proud (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). The humble in spirit will “lay hold upon honour” (Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary notes: “So near are extremes in life: the moment we are highest in our own imagination we are really lowest in power, in position, in prospect. He that would build lastingly must lay his foundation low.” (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Pulpit)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 24: *“A partner to a thief hates his own soul; he receives the oath, but does not testify.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** One who partners with a thief “hates his own soul” (see Proverbs 1:19)—he acts against his own life. “He heareth cursing” (KJV) or “the oath” (Ellicott) refers to the adjuration of a judge that anyone with knowledge of the theft must testify. The man hears the legal summons but remains silent, becoming an accomplice and sharing the thief’s punishment (Ellicott, Gill). The Pulpit Commentary notes that “all dishonesty or complicity with it is self-destructive.” (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill, Pulpit)
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-29.html
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 25: *“The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** The fear of man—worrying excessively about what people think—is a snare that traps many. It may even cost eternal life (Ellicott, citing Matthew 10:28; John 12:25). The contrast is trust in the LORD: that person “shall be safe”—set inaccessibly high, in the safest place imaginable (Enduring Word). The fear of man and trust in God are mutually exclusive postures.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm

- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** Preached a full sermon on this verse (No. 3080, 1874), calling it one of “two ancient proverbs” (with v.26). He noted: “The independent proposition, that the fear of man bringeth a snare, is a truth which experience…” (Sermon fragment from Bible Hub; full text unavailable from search). (Spurgeon)
  - https://mail.biblehub.com/sermons/proverbs/29-18.htm

- **Pulpit Commentary:** “The coward dies a thousand deaths; the brave, but once. Moral cowardice springs from want of inner conviction of the might of truth; moral strength, from the inner certainty that nothing but truth is victorious.” (Pulpit Homiletics)
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 26: *“Many seek the ruler’s favor, but a man receives justice from the LORD.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** Many seek advancement through a ruler’s favor, but the ruler’s approval is of little value because “every man’s judgment cometh from the LORD”—it is God who really decides each person’s worth (Ellicott, citing 1 Samuel 16:7; 1 Corinthians 4:5). Real justice and security come from God alone, not from human authorities (Enduring Word). This verse pairs naturally with v.25. (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/29.htm

---

## v. 27: *“An unjust man is detestable to the righteous, and one whose way is upright is detestable to the wicked.”*

- **Traditional Reading:** There is an unavoidable, fundamental divide between the righteous and the wicked—they are mutually “detestable” (an abomination) to each other. Light and darkness do not mix. The Pulpit Commentary calls this the “irreconcilable antagonism” between good and evil. This is not a call to hatred but an observation about the nature of the two ways of life. Ellicott notes this reflects the principle that “what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness?” (2 Corinthians 6:14). (Enduring Word, Ellicott, Gill, Pulpit)
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-29/

## Summary of Traditions and Distinctives Found

### Where Protestant traditions differ (v. 18 is the primary flashpoint):

| Tradition | Reading of v. 18 |
|---|---|
| **Traditional/Historic Protestant** (Gill, Henry, Ellicott, Barnes, Pulpit) | “Vision” = prophetic revelation/God’s Word preached. Without it, people run wild. |
| **Reformed** (The Gospel Coalition, Ligonier) | Strongly critiques the popular misapplication to “visionary leadership”; insists *chazon* = God’s revealed Word through prophets. |
| **Baptist** (Spurgeon, Gill, Garner-Howes) | Same as traditional: “vision” = preaching of the Word. Gill explicitly ties it to gospel preaching and the ordinary means of grace. |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word/David Guzik) | Affirms the traditional exegesis (*chazon* = prophetic revelation), explicitly rejecting the “visionary leadership” interpretation despite being in a tradition that values prophetic gifts. |
| **John Piper (Baptist/Reformed)** | Acknowledges the prophetic meaning but applies it more broadly to “godly dreaming” and Spirit-led imagination for mission. |
| **Modern Evangelical “Vision” Movement** | Popularly misapplies the KJV “where there is no vision, the people perish” to mean churches need vision statements and strategic plans. (Widely critiqued by the above.) |
